text:
Data Quality Assessment
While checking the statistics of the dataset, we noticed that some numerical features had extreme outliers, so we created boxplots to visualise the distribution of these features and identify the outliers that needed to be handled before proceeding with the analysis.


Code
# columns for boxplots
cols = ['score',
       'age',
       'equity',
       'balance',
       'salary']

# boxplots for numerical features
plt.figure(figsize=(8,7))
for i, col in enumerate(cols):
    sns.boxplot(bank_data[col], color=sns.color_palette('Set3')[i+1], ax=plt.subplot(3, 2, i+1))
    plt.title('Boxplot for {}'.format(col), fontsize=17)
    plt.xlabel(col)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









As expected, the balance sheet and salary data contain many outliers. The “equity” and “age” features also contain outliers, but they are few and small, so we decided to leave them unchanged. To more accurately determine which data to discard, we calculated the 95th, 97.5, and 99th percentiles. After this, we decided to discard balance and salary data at the 95th percentile.

title: Churn Analysis for Bank Customers
text:
Key Findings






TipMain Insights




Credit score is the strongest churn driver — as scores increase, so does the churn rate
Number of products reveals a clear pattern: customers with 1 product have only 10% churn, those with 2 products almost never leave, but customers with 3-4 products churn almost entirely
Age shows increasing churn from age 20 to 40, a small spike at 55, and almost no churn after 60
Recent activity correlates with churn — likely because customers transfer funds before closing accounts
Income and balance — customers with fewer funds are less likely to churn, while those earning above 45,000 show higher churn rates

title: Churn Analysis for Bank Customers
text:
Results
The analysis revealed several actionable patterns for the bank’s marketing department.
The bank successfully attracts credit and salary-transfer customers, but struggles to retain clients with other products. Customers with 3-4 products are almost entirely churned, suggesting that beyond credit services, the bank’s product offerings may not meet customer expectations.

The data suggests a critical gap: the bank lacks a compelling product for higher-income customers — the “upper middle class” segment earning above the regional average salary.

The relationship between recent activity and churn is particularly interesting. Customers who were recently active are more likely to leave, which makes sense — before closing an account, customers typically transfer their funds to other banks. This activity spike could serve as an early warning signal for the retention team.






WarningRecommendation



The bank should focus on developing premium products for customers with higher incomes (above 45,000) and consider personalised retention strategies for customers aged 30-45, who represent the highest churn risk segment.

title: BERT vs LLaMA 3: Fake News Detection
text:
Key Findings






TipMain Insights




BERT achieved 99.75% accuracy with perfect recall on fake articles — only 2 out of 800 articles were misclassified
LLaMA 3 achieved just 54% accuracy (barely above random chance) with a strong bias towards predicting “Real” — 23 out of 25 fake articles were missed
The performance gap is not a failure of LLaMA 3 as a model, but a limitation of few-shot prompting versus gradient-based fine-tuning for structured classification tasks









WarningBusiness Recommendation



For deployment in a news organisation’s editorial pipeline, BERT is the clear choice — its 99.75% accuracy translates to roughly 25 misclassifications per 10,000 articles. However, a hybrid architecture combining BERT’s classification reliability with LLaMA 3’s generative explainability could offer the best of both worlds: BERT flags articles, LLaMA 3 explains why.

title: BERT vs LLaMA 3: Fake News Detection
text:
Ethical Considerations
This project evaluated both models against the EU AI Act (2024) and Trustworthy AI principles. Key considerations include maintaining human oversight in editorial decisions, addressing dataset bias (the ISOT dataset reflects Western media perspectives), and ensuring transparency in model decision-making. LLaMA 3’s local deployment via Ollama offers a privacy advantage, as no article text leaves the organisation’s infrastructure.

title: Per-Item or Per-Posting? Modelling a Commission Grain Change
text:
A marketplace pays its pick-up point partners a commission on every item handed over to a customer: 5.5% of item value, capped at €2.50 per item.
Goods arrive at a pick-up point in postings — physical boxes. A box may hold one item or ten. The proposal is to move commission to posting grain: same percentage, but the cap applied once per box rather than once per item.
The finance question is what that costs or saves.
The analytical question is harder, and comes first: who pays for it? A cap that collapses from five charges to one affects a partner handling large consolidated boxes very differently from one handling single-item deliveries — and if the difference is large enough, an aggregate saving hides a retention risk in part of the network.






NoteData



Synthetic dataset of ~240,000 posting-item records across 850 pick-up locations and one calendar month. Data-quality defects — returns, superseded report versions, orders split across several boxes — were planted deliberately so the reconciliation steps have something real to catch. Generated by generate_data.py.

title: Per-Item or Per-Order? Modelling a Fee Grain Change
text:
A marketplace charges merchants a percentage fee on every item sold, capped per item. Finance wants to know what happens if the same fee is charged per order instead, with the cap applied once per order rather than once per item.
The question sounds like arithmetic. It isn’t. Changing the grain of a fee changes who pays it, and answering it correctly depends first on understanding how orders are actually composed.






NoteData



Synthetic dataset of ~249,000 order-item records across 400 merchants and one calendar month. Data-quality defects — reversals, superseded records, multi-shipment orders — were planted deliberately so the reconciliation steps have something real to catch.

title: Per-Item or Per-Posting? Modelling a Commission Grain Change
text:
A marketplace pays its pick-up point partners a commission on every item handed over to a customer: 5.5% of item value, capped at €2.50 per item.
Goods arrive at a pick-up point in postings — physical boxes. A box may hold one item or ten. The proposal is to move commission to posting grain: same percentage, but the cap applied once per box rather than once per item.
The finance question is what that costs or saves.
The analytical question is harder, and comes first: who pays for it? A cap that collapses from five charges to one affects a partner handling large consolidated boxes very differently from one handling single-item deliveries — and if the difference is large enough, an aggregate saving hides a retention risk in part of the network.






NoteData



Synthetic dataset of ~240,000 posting-item records across 850 pick-up locations and one calendar month. Data-quality defects — returns, superseded report versions, orders split across several boxes — were planted deliberately so the reconciliation steps have something real to catch. Generated by generate_data.py.




Setup
import duckdb
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_style("whitegrid")

RATE = 0.055
CAP = 2.50

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("CREATE VIEW fct_posting_items AS SELECT * FROM 'fct_posting_items.parquet'")
con.execute("CREATE VIEW dim_pickup_points AS SELECT * FROM 'dim_pickup_points.parquet'")

def q(sql):
    return con.execute(sql).df()

section: 1. Where the volume is, and where the value is
text:
1. Where the volume is, and where the value is
Before modelling anything, one table decides how the rest of the analysis has to be built.


Channel mix: postings, value, and box composition
mix = q("""
WITH clean AS (
    SELECT * FROM fct_posting_items
    WHERE record_status <> 'corrected'
      AND event_type NOT LIKE '%return%'
)
SELECT
    REPLACE(fulfilment_channel, '_', ' ')                  AS channel,
    ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT posting_id)
          / SUM(COUNT(DISTINCT posting_id)) OVER (), 1)    AS share_postings,
    ROUND(100.0 * SUM(item_value)
          / SUM(SUM(item_value)) OVER (), 1)               AS share_value,
    ROUND(COUNT(*) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT posting_id), 2)  AS items_per_posting,
    ROUND(SUM(item_value) / COUNT(DISTINCT posting_id), 2) AS avg_posting_value,
    ROUND(AVG(item_value), 2)                              AS avg_item_value
FROM clean
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY share_value DESC
""")

A commission per item follows value. A commission per box follows volume. Those are distributed differently — which is why a grain change moves money between channels rather than reducing it evenly.


Share of postings vs share of value
plot_df = mix.set_index("Channel")[["% postings", "% value"]].sort_values("% value")

ax = plot_df.plot(kind="barh", figsize=(8, 3.2), width=0.75,
                  color=["#99f0a2", "#99bbf0"])

Figure 1





The two right-hand columns explain the mechanism. Average item value runs from €4.37 in the warehouse channel to €21.33 in merchant shipped, while items per box runs the opposite way, from 3.6 down to 1.5. Cheap goods travel together; expensive goods travel alone.






ImportantWhat this means for the model



The cap is hit by box value, not item count. So the channels most exposed are those with the highest average posting value — merchant shipped and cross border, not warehouse.
Item count matters only at the edge: a box with one item cannot change at all, since per-item and per-posting are identical there.
Quantified in section 3.

text:
2. Getting to posting grain


What is in the raw data
prof = q("""
SELECT
    COUNT(*)                                                     AS rows_raw,
    COUNT(DISTINCT posting_id)                                   AS boxes,
    COUNT(DISTINCT pickup_point_id)                              AS points,
    SUM(CASE WHEN record_status = 'corrected' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS superseded,
    SUM(CASE WHEN event_type LIKE '%return%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)  AS returns_
FROM fct_posting_items
""")
prof.columns = ["Rows", "Boxes", "Pick-up points",
                "Restated rows", "Return rows"]

Restated rows are corrected partner reports — counting both versions inflates volume. Return rows are negative-signed mirrors — counting them as handovers inflates it again. And 18.8% of orders arrive as more than one box, so order grain is not a substitute for box grain.


Item grain to posting grain
con.execute("""
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW posting_grain AS
WITH clean AS (
    SELECT * FROM fct_posting_items
    WHERE record_status <> 'corrected'          -- drop restated reports
),
signed AS (
    SELECT
        posting_id, pickup_point_id, fulfilment_channel,
        CASE WHEN event_type LIKE '%return%' THEN -1 ELSE 1 END AS sign,
        item_value, item_commission
    FROM clean
)
SELECT
    posting_id,
    any_value(pickup_point_id)    AS pickup_point_id,
    any_value(fulfilment_channel) AS fulfilment_channel,
    SUM(item_value)               AS posting_value,
    SUM(item_commission)          AS commission_current,
    SUM(sign)                     AS items_net
FROM signed
GROUP BY posting_id
HAVING SUM(sign) > 0            -- a fully returned box earns no commission
   AND SUM(item_value) > 0
""")




Reconciling the re-aggregation
recon = q("""
WITH clean AS (
    SELECT * FROM fct_posting_items WHERE record_status <> 'corrected'
),
p AS (
    SELECT posting_id,
           SUM(item_value) AS v,
           SUM(CASE WHEN event_type LIKE '%return%' THEN -1 ELSE 1 END) AS n
    FROM clean GROUP BY posting_id
),
src      AS (SELECT COUNT(*) c, SUM(v) v FROM p),
orphan   AS (SELECT COUNT(*) c, SUM(v) v FROM p WHERE posting_id LIKE 'O9%'),
returned AS (SELECT COUNT(*) c, SUM(v) v FROM p
             WHERE posting_id NOT LIKE 'O9%' AND n <= 0),
final    AS (SELECT COUNT(*) c, SUM(posting_value) v FROM posting_grain)

SELECT 1 AS ord, 'Source: restated rows removed' AS step,
       src.c AS boxes, ROUND(src.v) AS val FROM src
UNION ALL SELECT 2, 'Less: returns with no handover in period',
       -orphan.c, -ROUND(orphan.v) FROM orphan
UNION ALL SELECT 3, 'Less: fully returned boxes',
       -returned.c, -ROUND(returned.v) FROM returned
UNION ALL SELECT 4, 'Posting grain, ready to model',
       final.c, ROUND(final.v) FROM final
ORDER BY ord
""").drop(columns=["ord"])

3. Modelling the change


Apply the proposed schedule
con.execute(f"""
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW modelled AS
SELECT
    *,
    LEAST(posting_value * {RATE}, {CAP})                       AS commission_proposed,
    LEAST(posting_value * {RATE}, {CAP}) - commission_current  AS delta
FROM posting_grain
""")

head = q("""
SELECT
    ROUND(SUM(commission_current))                              AS a,
    ROUND(SUM(commission_proposed))                             AS b,
    ROUND(SUM(delta))                                           AS c,
    ROUND(100.0 * SUM(delta) / SUM(commission_current), 1)      AS d
FROM modelled
""")

WarningThe aggregate hides the spread



The platform pays out 5.2% less. But the impact per partner runs from 0% to −14%, and 125 of 850 pick-up points lose more than 8% of their commission income.
Those are partners handling high-value goods in small boxes — the cross border and merchant shipped channels. A saving delivered by concentrating the loss on a tenth of the network is a retention question, not just a cost question.

title: Per-Item or Per-Posting? Modelling a Commission Grain Change
section: 4. How sensitive is this to where the cap sits?
text:
4. How sensitive is this to where the cap sits?


Rate and cap sensitivity
rows = []
for rate in [0.055, 0.060, 0.065, 0.070]:
    for cap in [1.50, 2.00, 2.50, 3.00, 4.00, 6.00]:
        r = q(f"""
            SELECT 100.0 * (SUM(LEAST(posting_value * {rate}, {cap}))
                            / SUM(commission_current) - 1) AS p
            FROM posting_grain
        """)
        rows.append({"rate": f"{rate:.1%}", "cap": f"€{cap:.2f}",
                     "pct": r["p"].iloc[0]})

grid = pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="rate", columns="cap", values="pct")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))
sns.heatmap(grid, annot=True, fmt=".1f", center=0, cmap="RdYlGn_r",
            cbar_kws={"label": "Change in payout (%)"}, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Green = platform pays less. Red = platform pays more.")
ax.set_xlabel("Per-posting cap")
ax.set_ylabel("Commission rate")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 5











ImportantThe cap does the work, not the rate



At the current 5.5% rate, break-even sits near a €3.20 per-posting cap. Set it looser and the change reverses: the existing €2.50 per-item cap already limits what expensive items earn, so a generous per-box cap removes that limit and payouts rise.
Every €0.50 of cap is worth roughly 4–5% of total payout. The rate is the visible number in a partner agreement; the cap is where the money is.

title: Per-Item or Per-Posting? Modelling a Commission Grain Change
text:
4. The result


Effect on the two metrics that matter
r = q("""
SELECT SUM(commission_current)  AS cur,
       SUM(commission_proposed) AS prop,
       SUM(delta)               AS d,
       SUM(posting_value)       AS val,
       SUM(items_net)           AS n_items
FROM modelled
""").iloc[0]

cur, prop, d = float(r.cur), float(r.prop), float(r.d)
val, n = float(r.val), float(r.n_items)

pd.DataFrame([
    ["Commission, % of goods value",
     f"{100*cur/val:.2f}%", f"{100*prop/val:.2f}%", f"{100*d/val:+.2f} pp"],
    ["Cost per item",
     f"€{cur/n:.3f}", f"€{prop/n:.3f}", f"{d/n:+.3f}"],
    ["Total commission, month",
     f"€{cur:,.0f}", f"€{prop:,.0f}", f"{d:+,.0f} ({100*(prop/cur-1):+.1f}%)"],
], columns=["", "Now", "After", "Change"])

TipFindings



Commission falls 5.2% — from 4.83% to 4.58% of goods value, or €0.29 to €0.28 per item handed over. Roughly €3,300 a month at current volumes.
The saving is structural, not a rate cut. The rate and the cap are unchanged. It comes entirely from a box of several items no longer being capped several times.
A box of one item is unaffected — per-item and per-posting are identical there. 19% of boxes fall in this group and contribute nothing to the saving.
The cost lands unevenly. Cross border and merchant shipped absorb ~9% each against warehouse’s 3.7%, and 125 of 850 partners lose more than 8% of their income.








WarningRecommendation




Proceed — the saving is real and comes from removing a duplication in how the cap is applied, not from paying partners a lower rate.
Model the 125 exposed partners individually before launch. A network average of −4.7% is not what they will experience.
Consider a transition floor for partners worse than −8%, funded from the saving. It costs a fraction of €3,300 a month and removes the retention risk.
Confirm the billing system can attach commission at posting level. The current logic prices per item; posting-level pricing needs the discount allocation moved from item to box.
Track realised versus modelled for the first two months. Box composition shifts with promotions, and the saving moves with it.

title: Per-Item or Per-Posting? Modelling a Commission Grain Change
text:
Method notes
Synthetic data throughout — no production data was used. DuckDB over parquet for the SQL, pandas and seaborn for modelling and charts, Quarto for the write-up.
Limitations: one month, so seasonality in box composition is untested; partners are assumed not to change behaviour in response to the new schedule; the model prices the change on today’s channel mix, which will drift.
